en: The Demonstration of Internal Pervasion (*Antarvyāptisamarthanam*).
Om, homage to the Buddha!
Here, existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency, because that which is other than this lacks the characteristic of existence.
And that [activity] is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, because these two are characterized by mutual exclusion;
for it is impossible to act in any other manner.
Furthermore, succession and simultaneity do not exist in that which is non-momentary.

Because it is impossible for that which possesses a single, unchanging nature across prior and subsequent times to have both agency and non-agency—two contradictory properties—there can be no succession [of actions] therein. For if there were succession, agency and non-agency would each apply to the entity at prior and subsequent times with respect to each individual action.
Thus, since all forms of succession are excluded, only the simultaneity of all effects remains as a possibility.
In that case, there follows the even more evident consequence of agency at the prior time and non-agency at the subsequent time.
Furthermore, contradictory states—agency and non-agency—cannot coexist in a single substratum.
And since it has been established that what possesses a single nature over that duration is non-momentary, it follows that neither succession nor simultaneity is possible for such a thing.

Thus, existence (*sattva*), having been negated in respect to the non-momentary by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), remains only in the momentary; therefore, it is pervaded by momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
That which is pervaded by it establishes momentariness wherever that [existence] is established in a given subject (*dharmin*).
This very point is now being investigated.
Where is this pervasion to be grasped: in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) or in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*)?
Some say:
It must exist in the subject of the example alone, like smoke;
otherwise, the proof would be futile, as both properties would not be established.
Because pervasion is established through the state of being inseparable from the subject (*ranāntarīyakatva*).
For once the pervasion between fire and smoke has been established in a kitchen, one does not again seek the mark of smoke for the sake of establishing fire. Thus it is said:
"Pervasion is grasped in the example between two properties that are observed therein."
The pervasion of the mere cause as it has been observed is understood in the subject (pakṣa).
And that [universal], through the inclusion of all [particulars], rests upon the universal;
its occurrence in the subject (dharmin), however, is to be understood through inference.

In the case of fire and smoke, which are perceived directly, the establishment of their causal relationship results in the establishment of their pervasion (vyāpti); thus, once fire is established by perception, it is logical that inference would be redundant.
It is not so here, for prior to the establishment of pervasion, momentariness is not established in the subject (dharmin) by any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Rather, perceiving only the probans (sādhanadharma) itself, we realize its pervasion with momentariness through the force of a subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa) against the contrary.
If it is argued that, therefore, the means of proof (sādhana) is futile—
indeed, it is futile because once existence, which is pervaded by momentariness, is cognized in the subject (dharmin) as being such, momentariness is also cognized therein— the answer is: no.

For pervasion (*vyāpti*), which encompasses all cases, is a constituent factor for the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, this [pervasion] relies solely upon the property that serves as the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*), without regard for the specific characteristics of the locus (*dharmin*).
For example:

Just as one says, "Where there is smoke, there is fire," and not, "Where there is smoke in the kitchen, there is fire," so too here, in the apprehension of the pervasion that "whatever exists is momentary," the presence of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) in the subject (*dharmin*) is not included within that [pervasion].
How much more so, then, for the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)?

Therefore, once the presence of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, the generality of existence (*sattvasāmānya*)—have been established individually, the occurrence of the property to be proven within the subject is understood through the force of both these factors. Thus, how can there be any futility in inference?

If that is so, [you might argue] that the apprehension of pervasion occurs in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) even in the absence of a reflective awareness (parāmarśa) regarding that subject.
Why?
Because the existence of the property observed therein is what brings about the cognition of pervasion.
Just as when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between fire and smoke is grasped in a kitchen, it is said that the grasping of pervasion occurs in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*);
for it has been stated that there is no further reflection upon the kitchen during the actual grasping of the pervasion.

Now, even if pervasion and the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmmatva*) are each cognized individually, since the pervasion with the probandum (*sādhya*) is already determined for that very thing whose status as a property of the subject is understood, the statement of the existence of the probandum is not redundant by virtue of its own implication (*sāmarthya*).
[This refers to] the means of proof (*sādhana*).

Now, is it not the case that the cognition of the property-to-be-proved (*sādhya*) is not the same as the cognition of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharman*), because [the latter] does not touch upon the property to be proved?
Nor is the mere apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself the establishment of the property to be proved.

Because the two properties are not delimited by a specific subject (*dharmin*) due to having a common objective support (*sāmānyālambanatā*), otherwise there would follow the consequence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two particulars. Therefore, this statement "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) is an indication of the reason (*hetu*) whose object is distributed.
Now, it may be said that the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) arises from the capacity to determine the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the reason.
In that case, the reason is not now useless,
because the ascertainment of the probandum arises from the ascertainment of its own nature;
for there is nowhere any further task to be performed by the logical mark beyond this.
Moreover, you maintain that inference occurs when the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) has been apprehended and the relationship (sambandha) has been remembered;
let it be accepted in the same way for internal pervasion (antarvyāpti).
For even among those who advocate external pervasion (bahirvyāpti), there is no operation of inference when the pervasion has been forgotten.

In that case, since the recollection of the pervasion by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) occurs only for that very [subject] whose status as a property of the locus (pakṣadharmatva) has been understood, why should there not be a total uselessness of all inference?
If it is argued that this is because the pervasion is remembered without a reflective awareness (aparāmarśa) of the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin),
then how can there be no reflective awareness of the subject of the thesis when the pervasion is remembered precisely of that which was perceived in the subject of the thesis?
If it is argued that [the pervasion] is not restricted because the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is not delimited due to the pervasion having a general object as its basis—
[we reply: how can that which is observed there not be delimited by it?
Alternatively, how can there be pervasion (vyāpti) for that which is delimited by such [a specific locus], since it would be over-exclusive (asādhāraṇa)?

If it is argued that it is not over-exclusive because the qualification is by way of exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda), even so, why is the subject of the probandum (sādhyadharmin) not apprehended?
For in the case of a pervasion whose object is a universal—such as "wherever there is smoke on a mountain, there is fire, as in a kitchen"—[the subject is indeed implied].

If it is argued that the specific consideration of the subject (*dharmī*) is not a constituent part [of the reason], this is correct; for the exclusion of non-connection with the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) is indeed another form of the probans (*sādhanadharma*), known as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).
However, this is not a constituent part of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Otherwise, since the determination of pervasion—which has the universal as its object—is completed even without that [subject], how could there even be talk of grasping the pervasion in the example-subject? For at that time, it would be impossible for it to be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

Or, if the property of the subject were grasped at that very moment, then by implication the unestablished probandum (*sādhya*) would also be established; thus, there would follow the absurd consequence that all inference is useless.
Furthermore, the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) occurring at a later time would merely be a memory and not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not a constituent part [of the reason], the property of being a subject-attribute (*pakṣadharmmatva*), even though it exists during the apprehension of pervasion, is not included therein. Thus, the cognition of the object to be inferred arises through the power of the property of being a subject-attribute and the pervasion, which have been apprehended and remembered separately. In this way, one must maintain that the means of proof (*sādhana*) are not redundant, because they constitute the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*māna*).

In the same way, why is it not accepted that the production of inference occurs through the power of the two—residence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and pervasion (*vyāpti*)—even when there is internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*)?
Or, if that is accepted, how can the means of proof (*sādhana*) be redundant?

For it is said that the "power" is precisely the capacity for its employment, since the comprehension of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) follows from the capacity for comprehending the three characteristics (*trairūpya*).
But it is not the case that [the property of being a reason] is included within the cognition of the three-fold character (trairūpya); thus, everything is the same.
[Reply: Not everything is the same.

For in internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is understood precisely through the understanding of the pervasion (vyāpti), because if the property of being a feature of the subject is not understood, the pervasion is also not understood.
Therefore, in a proof based on internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is useless when the pervasion is already established;

this is not so in the case of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*), because the apprehension of pervasion occurs only externally. To this, he says: "By whatever sequence that [pervasion] is applied here when the proof is employed..."
Having ascertained the property of the subject, the pervasion is subsequently cognized.
"If it were not so, how could that [invariable concomitance] exist in an example as if it were perceived directly?
If you say, 'We know [it exists] after seeing both,' then how could there have been a perception of both prior to the pervasion?
For pervasion and the property of being a subject (pakṣadharmatva) are indicated by whichever of one's own two statements is employed, but they are not cognized directly.
Because speech itself is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"The reason is an indicator of that which is capable [of proving], even though the speech itself is incapable.

Let there be, then, regarding the existence of those two [the probans and the subject] as indicated by that [speech], let the authority concerning the very first instance of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmmatva*) within the reason become manifest.

By that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the existence [of the reason] is established in the subject (*dharmin*); subsequently, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended by another means of valid cognition—so for whom, then, would there be redundancy?

Even in the case of perception, the reason is first apprehended in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), and afterwards the pervasion; this is precisely the sequence. Otherwise, it would not even be possible for the pervasion to be apprehended in the subject of the example, because one would be apprehending the pervasion of a reason that has not yet been seen in the subject of the example.
If it is argued that, in this case, the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) must likewise be apprehended in the locus where the pervasion is grasped—just as in the case of fire and smoke—we say no.
For in that instance, the pervasion is established merely by the presence of a subverting argument (bādhaka) against the reason in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
Furthermore, it is not known in this way; indeed, prior to the grasping of the pervasion, there is no proof whatsoever of momentariness anywhere, precisely because it is what is to be inferred.

Furthermore, since inference does not function when pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished, and one does not pursue another means of proof for that purpose; even if one were to pursue such a means, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
First, because effort would be futile if [the relationship] were merely one of coexistence;
second, because in the case of the reverse order, there is no obstruction to the establishment of pervasion by the very force of pervasion itself;
and third, because the causal relationship between fire and smoke is not established unless they have been previously perceived.

If that [pervasion] were established, would there not be a dependence on observing both [the presence in the similar class and the absence from the dissimilar class], since the operation of the subverting proof does not apply to the dissimilar class?
However, while the establishment of pervasion occurs between fire and smoke, it is not so for existence and momentariness;
for their pervasion is established by the reasoning already stated.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the pervasion (vyāpti) of mere existence, which is already established in that subject (dharmin), will be proven by virtue of the sublation [of its contrary];
the same applies to internal pervasion (antarvyāpti).

Thus, these two—pervasion and the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva)—are to be established in the proof-statement by means of their respective means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and are not merely to be indicated.
And since it is not possible for a single sentence to indicate both [meanings], how could one sentence be redundant?
For it is only through a sequence [of cognitions] that the threefold nature of a single entity is ascertained;
since there would be no inference in the case of forgetfulness, why then is all inference rendered useless?
Moreover, there is a summary verse:
"If the probandum is established by means of a subverting proof, the apprehension of another reason is useless;
if the probandum is not established by that subverting proof, the apprehension of another subject is useless."

For if the pervasion (vyāpti) were indeed established with respect to the subject (dharmin), it would necessarily include the establishment of the probandum (sādhyasiddhi). Is this not precisely a gain?
Since the probandum is established by the very same means of valid cognition that establishes the pervasion, the labor of resorting to the reason of "existence" (sattvahetu) is rendered superfluous.
For this pursuit of another mark is certainly not a calamity.

Now, if it is argued that the probandum is not established by that which proves the pervasion, then there is no pointlessness of the reason in the case of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*); so why do you undergo such excessive exertion out of groundless timidity?

For you, two things are to be proven: [the reason's] presence in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) and its presence in the subject-to-be-proven (*sādhyadharmin*), for the sake of establishing, respectively, pervasion (*vyāpti*) and being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Now, when there is a dispute regarding a specific subject...
Furthermore, if the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) were to occur in a subject (*dharmin*) external to that [subject under dispute], it would then be redundant.

However, when the dispute concerns the nature of reality (*vastumātra*) itself, then the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in all things must be established by both you and me; thus, in which subject would the proof of the reason's presence be redundant for me?
Moreover, how could there be "external pervasion" (*bahirvyāpti*), given that the establishment of pervasion occurs only in some one [subject] that has become the locus of the dispute?

If it is argued that because the subject (*dharmin*) is characterized by being merely that [the locus of the probandum], a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), even when operating within [the subject], excludes the subject from [the domain of] the definition; and if it is further argued: "How can this be so? For by the very operation of the subverting proof, the probandum is established in that [subject], and thus, since doubt regarding the probandum has been removed, the definition applies to the subject of the probandum"—this is incorrect.

In the position that the probandum is not established by the subverting evidence alone, it is stated that there is the futility of employing another subject (*dharmin*). However, in the position that the probandum is established by the subverting evidence, the futility of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is entailed.
Therefore, if the probandum is not established by the subverting evidence alone, doubt would never be dispelled.

When doubt has not been removed, the subject is not excluded, and since it is not excluded, it is indeed the very locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*); therefore, the pervasion therein is exclusively internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), and at this stage, there is not even a mention of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*).

Thus, how can this external pervasion occur in this [internal] case? It occurs if the dispute concerns a specific locus, while the apprehension of pervasion takes place with respect to a locus external to that.
Furthermore, in that case, there is the unavoidable fault of the uselessness of embracing another property (*dharmin*).

If the probandum were established by a mere sublation (*bādhaka*), then any other reason would be entirely redundant. Moreover, because the reason is a positive entity (*sat*), external pervasion (*vahirvyāpti*) is not possible.
Since there can be no entry into a dispute regarding the existence of the subject (*dharmin*) if it were non-existent,
and because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be grasped therein with respect to that which is non-existent in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
How could the apprehension of pervasion not occur, or how could it fail to exist even in the example?
For when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a reason (*hetu*) observed in a subject (*dharmin*) is cognized, that is called the "grasping of its pervasion.
And its existence in the subject to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) is indeed observed, since otherwise disagreement would be impossible; so how is it not "internal pervasion" (*antarvyāpti*)?

If you say, "Nevertheless, we grasp it only externally in order to avoid the futility of the means of proof," then, by your own admission, does the observation or non-observation of the reason in the subject now depend upon your mere whim?

Alternatively, let the determination of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occur only externally, even when there is a specific mode of perception. If it is argued that even when the apprehension of pervasion occurs for what is seen in both [internal and external] cases, there still exists a portion of external pervasion— well then,
for what purpose is such a large portion being preserved with such effort?
If it is argued that "the reason must not be rendered useless," [we reply:

surely, if the probandum is established in the subject (*dharmin*)—the locus for grasping the pervasion—merely by the operation of the subverting proof (*bādhaka*), then the uselessness of the means of proof (*sādhana*) in the case of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) applies equally to external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) as well. Therefore, the insistence on grasping external pervasion is merely a whim; specifically, in the case of the reason "existence" (*sattva*), the employment of a proof dependent upon an example occurs only out of necessity for the satisfaction of those with dull intellects.
For the sake of favoring those very individuals, the teacher provides an example:
"Whatever exists is momentary, just like a jar.
However, those of sharp intellect do not require such an example.
"Therefore, from among the examples already mentioned, he stated the jar as an example;
likewise, because it is not redundant among the means of valid cognition, let it be accepted even in the case of internal pervasion (antarvyāpti)."
Thus is the intermediate verse.

How, then, is the threefold nature (trairūpya) of the logical reason (hetu) to be understood as "certainty of existence in the subject alone," "existence only in the similar class (sapakṣa)," and "non-existence in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa)"?

[It is said: "The similar and dissimilar classes are considered to be those possessing or lacking the property to be proven (sādhyadharma); therein, the presence or absence of the reason is to be grasped, whether in those specific cases or wherever they may be."

Everything endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is, in general, the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), while that which is not so endowed is the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*). Existence only in that similar instance and non-existence in the dissimilar instance are, respectively, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). These two must be apprehended in whichever subject (*dharmin*) they can be apprehended, whether it be that very subject or another.

Thus, when it has been established through the force of sublation that existence here is excluded from everything non-momentary, the positive concomitance—that whatever exists is necessarily momentary—is apprehended in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).
This is because the pervasion (vyāpti) of the observed reason is grasped therein, as there is no possibility of another locus (dharmī);
and even if such a possibility existed, pursuing it would be useless.
If this is so, how is that which is called "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) stated to be "inconclusive" (anaikāntika)?

He stated that "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatā) is a fault of the reason from the perspective of a deluded person, because [the pervasion] is not grasped; however, this is not the case when there is a universal generalization (sarvopasaṃhṛti).
This has been stated: those of dull intellect have understood that the apprehension of pervasion occurs only within the subject itself (*dharmin*).
With regard to their misconception, [the author] declares "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) to be an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) because of the absence of an example.

Furthermore, since pervasion is not accepted [to exist] in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), and because when pervasion is unapprehended, it fails to produce certainty due to being "doubtful in both respects" (*sandigdhobhaya*), [it is inconclusive].
Alternatively, the claim that audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is unique [to sound] is merely fabricated by the conceit of the ignorant;
for it is indeed a specific instance of sound (*śabdavyakti*) that serves as the subject (*dharmin*), since it is the locus of the dispute.
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmyasiddhi*).
Furthermore, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is a reason that is common to both perceived and unperceived individual instances of sound,

just like the generality of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*). Consequently, because a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases is possible, the means of proof called audibility is indeed unperceived, just like existence (*sattva*) and other such reasons.
And in this case, the very non-perception of [the object] either successively or simultaneously is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
For "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) is simply the state of being a producer of auditory cognition;
therefore, it is an uncommon [reason] (*asādhāraṇa*) from the perspective of the deluded.
Because it is impossible to include all cases for that which is unique [to the subject],
and because the probandum would be cognized precisely upon the cognition of the pervasion in the subject of the probandum (sādhya-dharmin), the means of proof (sādhana) would necessarily be futile.
Lest this futility occur, one must not grasp the pervasion at all.

If that [pervasion] were not grasped, there would be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the ambiguity of both [the presence of the reason in the subject and its absence in the dissimilar instance].
However, when pervasion is grasped through a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), there is no futility of the proof (*sādhanavaiphalya*) according to the aforementioned reasoning;
therefore, it should be understood that existence (*sattva*) and other such reasons are indeed non-defective proofs.
Thus, in both ways, the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) has been stated with respect to the deluded person.
This is the same for those who maintain external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*): for if there were no regard for the views of the deluded, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) would indeed be a faultless reason.
For when there is a dispute regarding specific sounds, as in the case of "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth, there would be another sound [to serve as the locus].

Regarding all words, when a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) operates upon their absence [in the subject], it serves as a single example even where no example is seen; thus, how could there be an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) or "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason?
This concludes the demonstration of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*). // 0 //
This is the work of the venerable Ratnākaraśānti. // 0 //
